FitLoop — Growth model, backtest and 3 scenarios

Question for the board: is FitLoop's growth healthy, and where should the next euro go? This notebook turns the findings of analysis.ipynb into a forecasting model and uses it to compare the CEO's plan with two alternatives.

What the model does, in one line: ad spend → signups → activation → free trial → paying subscriber → churn / renewal → revenue, computed month by month and channel by channel.

What is in this notebook

Part Content

Read this first — what is exact and what is approximate. The raw CSV files were not available to the model builder, only the two notebooks. Everything that the notebooks printed (rates, Meta and Referral monthly series, quarterly totals, active subscribers, channel spend totals) is exact. The monthly signups of Google, Influencers, TikTok and Organic were read from the bar chart of the analysis notebook (error about ±15 users per month, then re-scaled so each quarter matches the exact total), and the monthly Google/TikTok spend was reconstructed from exact quarterly and channel totals. Part 3 lists this series by series. If you have the CSVs, replace these two tables (instructions in part 3) and re-run: nothing else changes.

1. The model — what it is and why it is built this way

1.1 The chain of the model (one box = one equation)

1.2 Plain-language explanation of each step (say this to the professors)

  1. Spend → signups. Each paid channel turns euros into signups. For Google, TikTok and Influencers we use a constant cost per signup (signups = spend ÷ CAC per signup), because the data gives only one total per channel. For Meta we have 17 monthly pairs (spend, signups), and they show diminishing returns: each extra euro buys fewer signups than the previous one (part 3). So Meta follows a power law signups = A × spend^β with β = 0.65. Organic does not depend on spend. Referral depends on the number of active subscribers (the growth loop, below).
  2. Signups → activation. A signup is activated if it does 3 workouts in 7 days. The activation rate depends on the channel (TikTok 16–24 %, Referral 48–67 %) and jumped on 1 Oct 2025 in every channel (finding 6 of the analysis). The model uses the "before" rate until Sept 2025 and the "after" rate from Oct 2025.
  3. Activation → trial → paid. The analysis shows two very different populations: activated users start a trial 59.6 % of the time and 43.9 % of those pay; non-activated users start a trial 10.0 % of the time and 15.9 % of those pay. So paid rate = a × 59.6 % × (43.9 % × m) + (1 − a) × 10.0 % × (15.9 % × m). m is a "channel quality" multiplier on trial→paid (TikTok 0.66, Referral 1.33, Google 1.12 …). It is calibrated so that the model gives back each channel's observed paid rate. It captures the fact that, given the same activation, a TikTok user is worth less than a Referral user.
  4. Timing. Paying starts at most 13 days after signup, so about one third of payers (assumption LAG = 33 %) pay for the first time in the month after their signup.
  5. Paid → churn. Monthly plan: each month a subscriber cancels with probability c (Referral 7 % … TikTok 17.5 %); this reproduces the retention table of the analysis (≈ 90 % after 1 month, ≈ 50 % after 6, ≈ 28 % after 12). Annual plan: 54 % renew each year. About 24 % of payers choose annual.
  6. Revenue = every payment made (9.99 € per month or 59.99 € per year). With these rules the lifetime value per payer is (1−annual)×9.99/c + annual×59.99/(1−0.54), exactly the formula of the analysis notebook (Google 118 €, Meta 101 €, TikTok 75 €, Referral 140 €).
  7. Growth loop. Referral signups = 86.7 + 0.041 × active subscribers (regression on the 18 monthly points of the analysis notebook). More subscribers → more referrals → more subscribers. In scenarios, the model recomputes the loop each month, so a scenario that creates more payers also creates more referrals.

1.3 Why a monthly cohort model?

Because a user who signs up today pays next month and keeps paying (or not) for many months. A cohort model keeps track of when each group of users signed up, so it can compute revenue, active subscribers and referrals at the right dates. A simple "signups × conversion × price" would ignore the delay and the churn.

1.4 Vocabulary used below

CAC = cost to acquire (a signup or a payer). LTV = total revenue a payer brings before leaving. β (elasticity) = by how many % signups grow when spend grows by 1 %. β = 1 means "twice the money = twice the users"; β < 1 means diminishing returns. Backtest = run the model on the past and compare it with what really happened. MAPE = mean absolute percentage error.

2. Inputs — the rates copied from the analysis notebook

Every number below is printed in analysis.ipynb (sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7). Nothing is estimated here except the multiplier m (explained) and the referral regression.

show code
# ---------- parameters from the analysis notebook
P = pd.DataFrame(index=CH)
P["act_pre"]  = [0.348,0.243,0.300,0.161,0.382,0.478]
P["act_post"] = [0.516,0.331,0.431,0.235,0.583,0.671]
P["act_all"]  = [0.442,0.273,0.380,0.213,0.497,0.598]
P["paid_obs"] = [0.140,0.071,0.113,0.045,0.156,0.216]
P["annual_share"] = [0.255,0.229,0.248,0.238,0.247,0.234]
P["churn"] = [0.088,0.128,0.109,0.175,0.087,0.070]
T_ACT,T_NON,P_ACT,P_NON = 0.596,0.100,0.439,0.159
RENEW = 0.54
LAG   = 0.33

def paid_rate(a, m):
    return a*T_ACT*np.minimum(1,m*P_ACT) + (1-a)*T_NON*np.minimum(1,m*P_NON)
raw = P.act_all*T_ACT*P_ACT + (1-P.act_all)*T_NON*P_NON
P["m"] = P.paid_obs/raw

def ltv(c):
    r=P.loc[c]; return (1-r.annual_share)*PRICE_M/r.churn + r.annual_share*PRICE_A/(1-RENEW)
P["ltv"] = [ltv(c) for c in CH]

3. Data used for the backtest — and how much to trust it

The backtest needs, for each month, the real spend and the real signups per channel, plus a few real "outcomes" (payers, revenue, active subscribers) to compare with.

show code
# ---------- actual series (exact from notebook outputs, or read from the notebook chart)
SIG = pd.DataFrame({
 'Google Ads': [532,471,410,454,495,495,395,395,601,583,480,542,889,704,580,602,643,622],
 'Influencers':[0,0,2498,0,0,0,0,0,2552,0,0,0,0,2655,0,0,0,0],
 'Meta Ads':   [780,773,677,732,773,838,738,827,1117,1004,1031,1161,1606,1292,1452,1332,1570,1655],
 'TikTok Ads': [0,0,0,0,0,1473,1173,1358,1811,1509,1385,1468,2120,1811,1523,1504,1483,1586],
 'Organic':    [589,447,406,430,450,471,391,370,638,558,558,558,926,741,638,639,639,700],
 'Referral':   [95,98,98,104,125,119,136,140,149,149,160,181,173,240,182,247,259,269]},index=HIST)[CH]

META_SPEND = pd.Series([3750,3270,2970,3240,3530,3850,3350,np.nan,5980,5430,5920,6450,10550,9200,8350,9110,9930,10820],index=HIST)

def reconstruct_spend():
    sp = pd.DataFrame(0.0,index=HIST,columns=PAID)
    sp["Meta Ads"] = META_SPEND
    for m in ["2025-03","2025-09","2026-02"]: sp.loc[pd.Period(m),"Influencers"]=9000.0
    qspend = {"2025Q1":26580,"2025Q2":20880,"2025Q3":35050,"2025Q4":36370,"2026Q1":60880}
    qspend["2026Q2"] = 229760-sum(qspend.values())          # Apr-Jun 2026 (Apr-May 32,370 + Jun 17,630)
    qlab = pd.Series([str(p.asfreq('Q')) for p in HIST],index=HIST)
    gt_q = {q: tot - sp.loc[qlab==q,"Meta Ads"].fillna(0).sum() - sp.loc[qlab==q,"Influencers"].sum() for q,tot in qspend.items()}
    col_tot = {"Google Ads":49810.0,"TikTok Ads":47250.0}      # exact channel totals from the analysis notebook
    X = pd.DataFrame({"Google Ads":SIG["Google Ads"]*5.29,"TikTok Ads":SIG["TikTok Ads"]*2.40},dtype=float)
    for _ in range(200):                                       # iterative proportional fitting (RAS)
        for q,t in gt_q.items():
            m=(qlab==q).values; X.loc[m]=X.loc[m]*t/X.loc[m].values.sum()
        for c,t in col_tot.items(): X[c]=X[c]*t/X[c].sum()
    sp[["Google Ads","TikTok Ads"]]=X
    return sp

# ---------- spend -> signups response (power law  S = A * spend^beta)
def fit_meta():
    s=META_SPEND.dropna(); y=SIG.loc[s.index,"Meta Ads"]
    b,a=np.polyfit(np.log(s),np.log(y),1); return np.exp(a),b
show code

3.1 Spend → signups: the Meta evidence for diminishing returns

elasticity beta = 0.647  (R2 = 0.979): +100% spend -> +57% signups.  Constant-CAC would give +100%.
Meta mean abs. % error: power law 3.5%  vs constant CAC 14.6%

Reading: with the power law the Meta error is about 3 %, with a straight line (constant CAC) about 15 %. The cost per Meta signup rose from ≈ 4.2 € to ≈ 6.5 € while the monthly budget almost tripled — this is the "Meta gets more expensive" finding of the analysis, now turned into a parameter. A doubling of the Meta budget gives only +57 % signups.

Honest limit: spend and time grow together in this data, so β = 0.65 is a measured association, not a proof of causality; and we have no such evidence for the other channels (their β is set to 1 in the base case and tested in the sensitivity analyses).

4. The engine

The code below runs the model month by month for the 30 months Jan 2025 → Jun 2027. For each month it (1) computes signups per channel, (2) applies activation, trial and paid rates, (3) puts the payers into their start month (with the 1-month lag), (4) follows each cohort with churn / renewal to get payments and active subscribers, and (5) feeds the number of active subscribers back into next month's referrals. The same function is used for the backtest and for all scenarios, so the scenarios differ from the baseline only by the inputs we change.

show code
def act_series(months, uplift_pts=0.0, uplift_start=None):
    """activation by channel and month: pre/post 1 Oct 2025 level (+ optional uplift in points)"""
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=months,columns=CH,dtype=float)
    for t in months:
        base = P["act_post"] if t>=pd.Period("2025-10") else P["act_pre"]
        up = uplift_pts if (uplift_start is not None and t>=uplift_start) else 0.0
        out.loc[t]=np.minimum(base+up,0.95)
    return out

def simulate(spend, organic, beta=None, uplift_pts=0.0, uplift_start=None, ref_loop=True, months=ALL):
    """Monthly cohort engine. spend: DataFrame(months x PAID, EUR); organic: Series(months)."""
    beta = {**BETA, **(beta or {})}
    T=len(months); idx={m:i for i,m in enumerate(months)}
    act = act_series(months,uplift_pts,uplift_start)
    S   = pd.DataFrame(0.0,index=months,columns=CH)
    start_m = {c:np.zeros(T+2) for c in CH}; start_a={c:np.zeros(T+2) for c in CH}
    ren_a = lambda k: RENEW**int((k-0.5)//12)                      # annual: share still active k months after start
    active_start = np.zeros(T+1)
    def active_at(u):
        tot=0.0
        for c in CH:
            ch=P.loc[c]
            for s in range(u):
                k=u-s
                tot += start_m[c][s]*(1-ch.churn)**(k-0.5) + start_a[c][s]*ren_a(k)
        return tot
    for t in range(T):
        m=months[t]; active_start[t]=active_at(t)
        for c in PAID:
            x=spend.loc[m,c]
            S.loc[m,c]= S_REF[c]*(x/REF[c])**beta[c] if x>0 else 0.0   # anchored power law
        S.loc[m,"Organic"]=organic.loc[m]
        S.loc[m,"Referral"]=(REF_A+REF_B*active_start[t]) if ref_loop else SIG.loc[m,"Referral"]
        for c in CH:
            ch=P.loc[c]; pay=S.loc[m,c]*paid_rate(act.loc[m,c],ch.m)
            for d,w in ((0,1-LAG),(1,LAG)):
                start_m[c][t+d]+=pay*w*(1-ch.annual_share); start_a[c][t+d]+=pay*w*ch.annual_share
    active_start[T]=active_at(T)
    # ---- outputs
    pay_rate = pd.DataFrame({c:[paid_rate(act.loc[m,c],P.loc[c,"m"]) for m in months] for c in CH},index=months)
    payers = S*pay_rate
    activated = S*act
    trials = pd.DataFrame({c:S[c]*(act[c]*T_ACT+(1-act[c])*T_NON) for c in CH})
    # payments matrix by signup cohort i and payment month j (EUR), per channel
    pm = {c:np.zeros((T,T)) for c in CH}
    for c in CH:
        ch=P.loc[c]
        for i in range(T):
            for d,w in ((0,1-LAG),(1,LAG)):
                n=payers.iloc[i][c]*w
                for k in range(T):
                    j=i+d+k
                    if j>=T: break
                    pm[c][i,j]+=n*(1-ch.annual_share)*(1-ch.churn)**k*PRICE_M
                for k in range(0,T,12):
                    j=i+d+k
                    if j>=T: break
                    pm[c][i,j]+=n*ch.annual_share*RENEW**(k//12)*PRICE_A
    rev_ch = pd.DataFrame({c:pm[c].sum(axis=0) for c in CH},index=months)
    return dict(S=S,act=act,activated=activated,trials=trials,payers=payers,pay_rate=pay_rate,
                active_start=pd.Series(active_start,index=months.append(pd.PeriodIndex([months[-1]+1]))),
                rev_ch=rev_ch,rev=rev_ch.sum(axis=1),pm=pm,spend=spend)

5. Backtest — predict Jan 2025 → Jun 2026 and compare with the real numbers

What we do. We give the model the real spend of each month (and real Organic signups, which are not driven by spend) and ask it to predict everything else. We then compare six outputs with the real numbers printed in the analysis notebook. Two of them (Meta signups, referral signups) are monthly; the others are monthly stocks or quarterly flows.

Fair-play rules (the same as the analysis notebook): payers and revenue are for the paid channels, signup quarters up to May 2026, and without the 827 Meta users of August 2025 (no spend known).

Honest status of the backtest. The rates come from the whole 18-month period, so this is an in-sample test: it proves the model's structure and arithmetic are consistent with the data (timing, churn, loop, activation break). It is not an out-of-sample forecast test. Two things are not predicted but given: Organic signups, and the October 2025 activation jump (a structural break that nobody could have forecast).

def stats(name,pred,act):
    pred=np.asarray(pred,float);act=np.asarray(act,float); m=act>0
    return dict(check=name,n=int(m.sum()),MAPE=np.mean(np.abs(pred[m]/act[m]-1)),bias=pred[m].sum()/act[m].sum()-1)

Reading the results. - Signups per quarter: error ≈ 1 %. Spend, response curve and loop together explain total signups. - Meta signups: ≈ 3 %, referral signups: ≈ 6 % — the growth loop and the diminishing-returns curve both work. - Active subscribers: ≈ 1.6 % (4,135 predicted vs 4,141 real on 1 June 2026). This is the strongest test: it combines signups, activation, conversion, plan mix, monthly churn, annual renewal and timing. - Payers and revenue by signup quarter: ≈ 5–6 %. The weakest point is 2025 Q3 (the notebook's "worst cohort"): the model under-predicts payers of the paid channels by about 14 %, because it splits payers between paid and organic channels a bit differently from reality. We keep this visible instead of hiding it. - Bias is close to zero (signed error ≤ 2 %): the model is not systematically too optimistic or too pessimistic.

Sentence to use: "Over 18 months the model reproduces quarterly signups within 1 %, the subscriber base within 2 %, and payers and revenue within about 6 %."

6. Baseline forecast — July 2026 → June 2027, budget unchanged

The three scenarios are compared with this baseline. Baseline assumptions: - Spend continues at the April–June 2026 run-rate per channel (Google, Meta, TikTok), and Influencers at its historical average of 1,500 € per month (27,000 € in 18 months). Total ≈ 18,170 € per month, 218,000 € per year. - Organic stays flat at the Q2 2026 level (≈ 660 signups per month). This is conservative: organic grew about 50 % year on year and has peaks in January and September. Because it is identical in every scenario, it changes levels but not the differences between scenarios. - Activation stays at its post-October 2025 level; churn, plan mix and renewal as in the analysis; referrals follow the growth loop.

show code
# ---------- scenarios
ORG_FLAT = SIG["Organic"].iloc[-3:].mean()
ORGANIC_ALL = pd.Series(SIG["Organic"].tolist()+[ORG_FLAT]*len(FC),index=ALL)
_last3 = SPEND_HIST.iloc[-3:].mean()
BASE_FC = pd.DataFrame({"Google Ads":_last3["Google Ads"],"Influencers":27000/18,"Meta Ads":_last3["Meta Ads"],"TikTok Ads":_last3["TikTok Ads"]},index=FC)

def run(fc_spend=None, **kw):
    fc_spend = BASE_FC if fc_spend is None else fc_spend
    sp = pd.concat([SPEND_HIST,fc_spend])
    return simulate(sp,ORGANIC_ALL,months=ALL,**kw)

def horizon_summary(r):
    h=FC; S=r["S"].loc[h]; pay=r["payers"].loc[h]; sp=r["spend"].loc[h]
    ltv_new=(pay*P["ltv"]).sum().sum()
    out=dict(spend=sp.sum().sum(), signups=S.sum().sum(), activated=r["activated"].loc[h].sum().sum(),
             trials=r["trials"].loc[h].sum().sum(), new_payers=pay.sum().sum(), paid_ch_payers=pay[PAID].sum().sum(),
             revenue=r["rev"].loc[h].sum(), active_end=r["active_start"].iloc[-1], ltv_new=ltv_new)
    out["cac_per_payer"]=out["spend"]/out["paid_ch_payers"]
    out["rev_minus_spend"]=out["revenue"]-out["spend"]
    out["ltv_minus_spend"]=out["ltv_new"]-out["spend"]
    return pd.Series(out)

How we compare scenarios. We report, over the 12 forecast months: ad spend, signups, activated users, trials, new paying users, cash revenue collected in the 12 months, and the lifetime value (LTV) of the new paying users. We use both revenue and LTV because a payer acquired in month 11 has paid almost nothing by month 12 but will keep paying for ~10 months; looking only at 12-month cash would penalise every scenario that acquires users. LTV is undiscounted and counts only ad spend as a cost (no salaries, no store fees) — good for comparing options, not an absolute profit.

show code
FLAB={"spend":"Ad spend (EUR)","signups":"Signups","activated":"Activated (3 workouts / 7 days)","trials":"Free trials started","new_payers":"New paying users (all channels)",
 "revenue":"Cash revenue in the 12 months (EUR)","active_end":"Active subscribers at end of horizon","ltv_new":"Lifetime value of the new payers (EUR)",
 "cac_per_payer":"CAC per payer, paid channels (EUR)","rev_minus_spend":"Revenue minus ad spend, 12 months (EUR)","ltv_minus_spend":"Lifetime value minus ad spend (EUR)"}
def compare(r_base,r_scn,name):
    a,b=horizon_summary(r_base).drop("paid_ch_payers"),horizon_summary(r_scn).drop("paid_ch_payers")
    t=pd.DataFrame({"Baseline":a,name:b}); t["Change"]=t[name]-t["Baseline"]; t["Change %"]=t["Change"]/t["Baseline"].abs()
    t.index=[FLAB[i] for i in t.index]; return t
def funnel_rates(r):
    h=FC; s=r["S"].loc[h].sum().sum()
    return pd.Series({"activation rate":r["activated"].loc[h].sum().sum()/s,"trial rate (of signups)":r["trials"].loc[h].sum().sum()/s,"signup -> paid":r["payers"].loc[h].sum().sum()/s})
def scenario_charts(r0,r1,name):
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(13,8)); ax=axs.ravel(); H=FC.astype(str)
    cats=["Google Ads","Meta Ads","TikTok Ads","Influencers"]; w=0.38; x=np.arange(len(cats))
    for k,(r,lab,off,al) in enumerate([(r0,"Baseline",-w/2,0.45),(r1,name,w/2,1.0)]):
        ax[0].bar(x+off,[r["spend"].loc[FC,c].sum() for c in cats],w,color=[COLOR[c] for c in cats],alpha=al,label=lab,edgecolor="white")
    ax[0].set_xticks(x,cats); ax[0].set_title("12-month ad spend by channel (pale = baseline)"); ax[0].yaxis.set_major_formatter(eur)
    cats2=CH; x2=np.arange(len(cats2))
    for r,off,al in [(r0,-w/2,0.45),(r1,w/2,1.0)]:
        ax[1].bar(x2+off,[r["payers"].loc[FC,c].sum() for c in cats2],w,color=[COLOR[c] for c in cats2],alpha=al,edgecolor="white")
    ax[1].set_xticks(x2,[c.replace(" Ads","") for c in cats2]); ax[1].set_title("New paying users by channel (pale = baseline)")
    ax[2].plot(H,r0["payers"].loc[FC].sum(axis=1),color=MUTED,label="Baseline"); ax[2].plot(H,r1["payers"].loc[FC].sum(axis=1),color="#2a78d6",label=name)
    ax[2].set_title("New paying users per signup month"); ax[2].tick_params(axis="x",rotation=60); ax[2].legend(); ax[2].set_ylim(0)
    c0=r0["rev"].loc[FC].cumsum(); c1=r1["rev"].loc[FC].cumsum()
    ax[3].plot(H,c0,color=MUTED,label="Baseline"); ax[3].plot(H,c1,color="#2a78d6",label=name); ax[3].fill_between(H,c0,c1,color="#2a78d6",alpha=0.12)
    ax[3].set_title("Cumulative cash revenue"); ax[3].tick_params(axis="x",rotation=60); ax[3].yaxis.set_major_formatter(eur); ax[3].legend()
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
def fmt(t):
    f=t.copy().astype(object)
    for i in t.index:
        for c in ["Baseline",t.columns[1],"Change"]: f.loc[i,c]=f"{t.loc[i,c]:,.0f}" if abs(t.loc[i,"Baseline"])>200 else f"{t.loc[i,c]:,.1f}"
        f.loc[i,"Change %"]=f"{t.loc[i,'Change %']:+.0%}"
    return f

7. Scenario 1 — double the budget with the same mix (the CEO's plan)

Idea. Spend twice as much on each channel, in the same proportions: 218,000 € → 436,000 € per year.

Mechanism in the model. Each channel gets 2× the money. Meta follows its measured curve (β = 0.65 → +57 % signups). For Google, TikTok and Influencers there is no measured curve, so the base case assumes no saturation (β = 1: twice the money, twice the signups) — this is the optimistic version for the CEO. The sensitivity just below stresses it.

Reading. - Doubling the budget gives +69 % signups and +56 % new payers, not +100 %, mainly because Meta saturates and because the extra money goes mostly to TikTok and Meta, the two channels with the weakest conversion. - The average CAC per payer rises (45 € → 51 €) and the marginal CAC of the extra 218,000 € is about 55 € per extra payer, against an average LTV of about 100 € per payer: the extra money still earns more than it costs (≈ 1.8 € of lifetime value per extra euro), but with a long payback (≈ 6 months) and little margin for error. - Over the first 12 months, cash revenue rises by about 181,000 € for 218,000 € extra spend: it does not pay back within the year; it pays back only through the LTV of users acquired.

Stress test. If Google, TikTok and Influencers saturate like Meta (β = 0.65 for all), the extra money earns only ≈ 1.3 € of LTV per euro and the marginal CAC rises to about 77 € per payer. The CEO's plan is not a disaster, but it is the least efficient use of a euro, and its result depends entirely on an assumption (no saturation) that FitLoop has never tested.

What to say: "Doubling is positive on paper but buys weaker users at higher marginal cost; the more we double, the more the answer depends on diminishing returns, which we measured on Meta (β = 0.65) and cannot rule out on the others."

8. Scenario 2 — same budget, move money from TikTok to Google Ads

Idea. TikTok has the cheapest signup (≈ 2.3 €) but the worst payers: only 4.5 % of its signups pay, they leave fastest (17.5 % churn per month) and their LTV is 75 €. Google costs ≈ 5 € per signup but 14 % of its signups pay and LTV is 118 €. We move 100 % of the TikTok budget (≈ 3,590 € per month) to Google; total spend is unchanged (218,000 €).

Mechanism in the model. TikTok signups fall to zero; Google receives ≈ 2.15× its former budget. In the base case Google keeps a constant cost per signup (β = 1) — again the optimistic ceiling, since doubling a channel's budget normally lowers its efficiency. The sensitivity table below answers "how much saturation can Google take before the move stops being worth it?"

show code

Reading. - The model shows fewer signups (−16 %) but more paying users (+7 %, about +500): we trade volume for quality. The CEO would see a "drop in growth" even though the business improves — a good point for the discussion on the North Star Metric (activated users or payers, not signups).

# What if Google saturates? Test different elasticities (beta) for the enlarged Google budget
def d_payers_ltv(fc,be):
    h=horizon_summary(run(fc,beta={"Google Ads":be})); return h.new_payers-hb.new_payers,h.ltv_new-hb.ltv_new

Robustness — the break-even. Moving 100 % of TikTok to Google is worth it only if Google keeps an elasticity above ≈ 0.73 (in number of payers) or above ≈ 0.51 (in lifetime value, because Google payers stay longer). Meta, the only channel we measured, has 0.65: on that curve you would get about 130 fewer payers but still about +24,000 € of lifetime value. Moving only 25–50 % is safer: even in the pessimistic column the loss is small (< 40 payers) and the LTV is still higher.

What to say: "Scenario 2 is positive in the base case and positive in lifetime value even under Meta-like saturation, but it is a hypothesis about Google's capacity. We would not move 100 % at once: we would move 25 %, measure Google's marginal CAC, then continue."

9. Scenario 3 — same budget, improve activation

Idea. Keep the 218,000 € and the mix unchanged; improve onboarding so that 5 more users out of 100 do 3 workouts in their first week (from ≈ 41 % to ≈ 46 % on average), in every channel, starting July 2026.

Why +5 points? On 1 Oct 2025 activation jumped by about 14 points overnight (from about 26 % to about 40 %), so a +5 point improvement is a modest target, and the analysis shows activation is the strongest predictor of payment (an activated user is 17× more likely to pay). It is a hypothesis to test, not a forecast.

Mechanism in the model. Activation of each channel goes up by 5 points. Because activated users convert 16× better than the others (26 % vs 1.6 % to paid), the paid rate rises everywhere, including Organic and Referral users — and more subscribers also create more referrals through the loop.

Reading. - With no extra euro, the model gives about +740 new payers (+10 %), +34,000 € of revenue in the first 12 months and +77,000 € of lifetime value. - CAC per payer falls from 45 € to 41 €, because the same advertising now produces more payers. - Unlike Scenario 2 it does not rely on an untested channel response: it relies on the activation → payment relation, which the analysis measured and found stable before and after October 2025 (26.2 % and 26.1 % for activated users). - It also benefits all channels, including the organic and referral ones that cost nothing.

Sensitivity. The table shows different sizes of effect and a realistic delay: if the improvement only starts in October 2026 (after a 3-month A/B test and roll-out), the gain is about 25 % smaller. The last table gives the A/B test size: to detect +5 points with 80 % power you need about 1,500 users per group, i.e. about 18 days of traffic — a fast and cheap test, which fits the A/B test plan required in the report.

Reading the comparison. - S1 creates the most value in absolute terms (+398,000 € of LTV) but needs +218,000 € and nets about +180,000 €; and it is the scenario most exposed to saturation (stress case: net ≈ +66,000 €, see part 7). - S2 and S3 need no additional money and create about +99,000 € and +77,000 € of lifetime value. They are free options, so their return per euro is not defined (infinite) — but they carry execution risk (Google's capacity for S2, the product team's ability to lift activation for S3). - The three are not mutually exclusive: S3 improves the value of every signup, which makes S1 and S2 better; S2 improves the mix, which makes S3 (applied to better users) and S1 better.

Recommendation (what we would tell the board)

  1. Do not double the budget now. The growth is real, but the extra euro buys the weakest users; the plan depends on an untested assumption (no saturation), and the average CAC is already rising on Meta.
  2. First, test and ship activation (S3). It is the cheapest and fastest lever: a test of ≈ 18 days, a measured mechanism, a benefit on every channel. Make "activated users" the North Star Metric (analysis finding 8).
  3. Shift budget gradually from TikTok to Google (S2): 25 % first, track Google's marginal CAC per payer, then continue if it stays below the break-even.
  4. Then scale spend step by step (e.g. +25 % at a time) on the channels with the best LTV/CAC (Google, referral programme tests), instead of ×2 in one go.

Limits of the model (be the first to say them)

Limit Effect How to improve
Monthly Google/TikTok/Organic signups and Google/TikTok spend are approximate (chart reading, reconstruction) small error on the backtest inputs, none on the exact comparison targets replace with the CSV tables (part 3)
In-sample backtest proves consistency, not predictive power re-estimate on 2025 only and predict 2026 (needs the CSVs)
Constant CAC for Google/TikTok/Influencers S1 and S2 are optimistic ceilings measure with a geo or time split test
Constant churn per channel, annual renewal 54 % LTV may differ for new cohorts (the analysis saw no improvement in retention) add cohort-specific churn
Organic flat, no seasonality levels are conservative add seasonal factors with 24+ months
LTV undiscounted, only ad spend as cost overstates absolute profit add discount rate, store fees (15–30 %), costs
The Oct 2025 activation jump is unexplained S3's +5 points is a hypothesis find the cause, then A/B test
Scenario interactions (e.g. brand effects of TikTok on organic) ignored possible hidden value of TikTok track organic after the shift

"Cold question" cheat-sheet

Q1. Why is your model not just conversion × price? Because users pay after signup and then leave at different speeds; the cohort structure gives revenue and subscribers at the right dates, and it is what lets the referral loop work.

Q2. How do you know the model is right? The backtest: it reproduces total signups (≈ 1 %), the subscriber base (≈ 2 %), payers and revenue (≈ 6 %) with no bias, and it explains the paid-rate change after October 2025 from the activation change alone (error 0.4 point). Limits: in-sample, and we say so.

Q3. Why is doubling the budget not +100 % signups? Diminishing returns: on Meta, cost per signup rose from 4.2 € to 6.5 € while spend tripled (β = 0.65). The extra money also goes to weaker channels.

Q4. Your S2 says TikTok → Google is good. What if Google saturates? It stays positive in lifetime value down to an elasticity of 0.51, and positive in payers down to 0.73; Meta's measured 0.65 lies between. That is why we recommend a staged 25 % move.

Q5. Why +5 points of activation? It is one third of what happened on 1 Oct 2025 (+14 points). It's a target to test, with about 1,500 users per arm needed.

Q6. Why not look at revenue only? Twelve-month cash penalises growth: a payer acquired in month 11 has paid once. LTV values the whole stream; we show both.

Q7. What is the least reliable assumption? No saturation on Google, TikTok and Influencers (S1, S2), then organic held flat. Neither changes the ranking conclusion that spend is the least efficient lever.

Q8. What would you do with one more month? Replace the approximate series with the CSVs, run an out-of-sample backtest (fit on 2025, predict 2026), and add churn by cohort.
